title: Definition
body_md:
For \(n\ge 3\), a {\em weak generalised $n$-gon} is a point-line geometry satisfying:   
	\begin{enumerate}[(GP1)]
		\item There exists no \(k\)-gon (as a subgeometry) for \(2 \le k < n\).
		\item Every two elements of \(\mathcal{P} \cup \mathcal{L}\) are contained in an \(n\)-gon.
	\end{enumerate}
head: environment

title: Definition
body_md:
A {\em thick generalised \(n\)-gon} is a weak generalised \(n\)-gon with the additional property:
	\begin{enumerate}[(GP3)]
		\item There exists an \((n+1)\)-gon (as a subgeometry).
	\end{enumerate}

title: Definition
body_md: The \(\mathbb{F}\)-ary code of the generalised polygon, denoted by \(\mathfrak{C}_{\mathbb{F}}(\Gamma)\), is the vector subspace of \(\mathbb{F}\mathcal{P}\) generated by \(\{\mathfrak{i}_L\mid L\in\mathcal{L} \}\). The {\em dual} code, denoted by \(\mathfrak{C}_\mathbb{F}^D(\Gamma)\) is the dual of this subspace (as defined in Definition \ref{def}).
head: environment

label: BS
title: Theorem
body_md:
(Bagchi \& Sastry \cite{BandS})\label{BS}
	Let \(\Gamma\) be a finite thick generalised \(2m\)-gon of order \((s,t)\) with \(m\ge2\). Let \(\mathbb{F}\) be any field. Then:
	\begin{enumerate}[(i)]
		\item The minimum weight of \(\mathfrak{C}_\mathbb{F}^D(\Gamma)\) is at least \(2(t^m-1)(t-1)^{-1}\). 
		If \(\Gamma\) is \emph{regular}, then equality holds.
		\item The minimum weight of \(\mathfrak{C}_\mathbb{F}(\Gamma)\) is at most \(s+1\). If \(\Gamma\) is \emph{regular}, then equality holds and any word of weight \(s+1\) is of the form \(\lambda\cdot\mathfrak{i}_L\) for some \(0\neq\lambda\in \mathbb{F}\) and some line \(L\).
	\end{enumerate}
head: environment

label: AK
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{AK}(Assmus \& Key \cite[Theorem 6.3.1 and Corollary 5.7.5]{AssmusAndKey})
	Let $\mathbb{F}=\mathbb{F}_p$, $p$ prime and let \(\Gamma\) be the geometry of points and lines in $\Pi$, where $\Pi$ is an arbitrary projective plane whose order $q$ is a multiple of $p$, or $\Pi$ is the projective geometry $\mathrm{PG}(k,q)$, $q=p^h$. Then the minimum weight of \(\mathfrak{C}_\mathbb{F}(\Gamma)\) is \(q+1\) and the code words of minimum weight are scalar multiples of incidence vectors of lines.
head: environment

label: remarkfield
title: Remark
body_md:
\label{remarkfield}
It is important to remark that the code \(\mathfrak{C}_\mathbb{F}(\Gamma)\), where $\Gamma=\mathrm{PG}(k,q)$ is {\em trivial} when $\mathbb{F}$ is a finite field whose characteristic is different from $p$ (see e.g. \cite[Theorem 2.5]{SurveyCodes}); in this context, trivial means that the code is either the full space or the dual of the all-one vector. Note that the minimum distance of a trivial code is $1$ or $2$ respectively, which is strictly smaller than $q+1$, the weight of the incidence vector of a line.
head: environment

label: cor:embedded
title: Corollary
body_md:
\label{cor:embedded}
	Let \(\Gamma\) be a weak generalised \(n\)-gon which is fully embedded in $\mathrm{PG}(k, q)$ and let \(\mathbb{F}\) be the field \(\mathbb{F}_p\) where \(p\) is a divisor of \(q\). Then the minimum weight of \(\mathfrak{C}_\mathbb{F}(\Gamma)\) is \(q+1\).
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md: The code \(\mathfrak{C}_\mathbb{F}(\Gamma)\) is a subspace of the code \(\mathfrak{C}_\mathbb{F}(\Gamma')\), where $\Gamma'$ is the geometry of points and lines from $\mathrm{PG}(k,q)$. It follows from Theorem \ref{AK} that \(q+1\) is a lower bound for the minimum weight of \(\mathfrak{C}_\mathbb{F}(\Gamma)\), and the incidence vector of any line of \(\Gamma \) shows equality.
head: environment

title: Remark
body_md: Corollary \ref{cor:embedded} has two strong requirements which make its use rather limited: not all weak generalised polygons are embeddable in a projective space $\mathrm{PG}(k,q)$, and even for those who are embeddable, Corollary \ref{cor:embedded} doesn't say anything about the case where $\mathbb{F}$ is different from $\mathbb{F}_p$. It can be seen from Theorem \ref{BS} that it is not because the code \(\mathfrak{C}_\mathbb{F}(\mathrm{PG}(k,q))\) is trivial for $\mathbb{F}\neq \mathbb{F}_p$ that its subcode \(\mathfrak{C}_\mathbb{F}(\Gamma)\) is trivial (if it would, the minimum weight would be at most $2$). Furthermore, one should also not deduce from Theorem \ref{AK} that all minimum-weight vectors of \(\mathfrak{C}_\mathbb{F}(\Gamma)\)  necessarily correspond to lines of $\Gamma$; it only follows that the minimum weight vectors correspond to point sets arising from a line of the ambient projective space.
head: environment

label: BoseBurton
title: Theorem
body_md:
(Bose \& Burton \cite{BoseBurton})\label{BoseBurton}
A set $B$ of points of $\mathrm{PG}(k,q)$ blocking all hyperplanes has at least the size of a line, and equality holds if and only if the set $B$ is the point set of a line.

label: GammaSets
title: Definition
body_md:
\label{GammaSets}\label{def:GammaSets}
	Let $\Gamma=(\mathcal{P},\mathcal{L}, \mathtt{I})$ be a point-line geometry and let $x$ be an element of $\Gamma$. We define the following sets:
	\begin{align*}
		\Gamma_i(x) &:= \{y \in \mathcal{P}\cup \mathcal{L} : \delta(x,y) = i\}, \\
		\Gamma_{\le i}(x) &:= \{y \in \mathcal{P}\cup\mathcal{L}: \delta(x,y) \le i\}, \\
		\mathcal{P}_i(x) &:= \{y \in \mathcal{P}: \delta(x,y) = i\}, \\
		\mathcal{P}_{\le i}(x) &:= \{y \in \mathcal{P}: \delta(x,y) \le i\}, \\ 
		\mathcal{L}_i(x) &:= \{y \in \mathcal{L}: \delta(x,y) = i\}, \\
		\mathcal{L}_{\le i}(x) &:= \{y \in \mathcal{L}: \delta(x,y) \le i\} ,
	\end{align*}
	where \(\delta(x,y)\) is the distance between \(x\) and \(y\) (inherited from the incidence graph).
head: environment

label: gammaProperties
title: Corollary
head: environment

label: intersections1
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{intersections1}
	Let \(x\) be an element of $\Gamma$. Let $y_1, y_2$ be elements with $\delta(x,y_1)=\delta(x,y_2)=d_1$ and $\delta(y_1,y_2)=2d_1$ with \(d_1\in\{1,\dots,m-1\}\). 
    
    Let \(d_2\in\{1,\dots,2m-d_1-1\}\).
                                                                                                                                        
	                                            
	Then,
	\[\Gamma_{\le d_2-d_1}(x) = \Gamma_{\le d_2}(y_1)\cap\Gamma_{\le d_2}(y_2).\]
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
We clearly have that
	\[\Gamma_{\le d_2-d_1}(x) \subseteq \Gamma_{\le d_2}(y_1)\cap\Gamma_{\le d_2}(y_2).\]
	Now assume that there is an element \(z\) in \(\Gamma_{\le d_2}(y_1)\cap\Gamma_{\le d_2}(y_2)\) with \(z\not\in\)  \(\Gamma_{\le d_2-d_1}(x)\). Then, combining the paths from \(z\) to \(y_1\), from \(y_1\) to \(y_2\) and from \(y_2\) back to \(z\), we find a cycle of length at most \(d_2 + 2d_1+ d_2 \le 4m-2d_1-2+2d_1 = 4m-2.\) This contradicts Theorem \ref{incidenceGraph} which states that the incidence graph of a \(2m\)-gon has girth \(4m\).
head: environment

label: intersections2
title: Corollary
body_md:
\label{intersections2}
\begin{enumerate}[(i)]
\item 	Let \(x\) be an element of $\Gamma$. Let \(y_1\neq y_2 \in \Gamma_1(x)\) and let \(d\in\{1,\dots,2m-2\}\).
	Then,
	\[\Gamma_{\le d - 1}(x) = \Gamma_{\le d}(y_1)\cap\Gamma_{\le d}(y_2).\]

\item  Let \(L\) be a line of \(\Gamma\) and let \(r\in \{1,2,\dots,m-1\}\).
	\begin{enumerate}[(a)]
		\item If 
		\(M_1\) and \(M_2\) are two disjoint lines intersecting \(L\),
		then
		\[\mathcal{P}_{\le 2r-3}(L) = \mathcal{P}_{\le 2r-1}(M_1)\cap\mathcal{P}_{\le 2r-1}(M_2).\]
		\item If
		\(v_1\) and \(v_2\) are two distinct points on \(L\), then
		\[\mathcal{P}_{\le 2r-1}(L) = \mathcal{P}_{\le 2r}(v_1)\cap\mathcal{P}_{\le 2r}(v_2).\]
	\end{enumerate}
\end{enumerate}
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
\begin{enumerate}[(i)]
\item 	This follows from Lemma \ref{intersections1} with \(d_1 = 1\).
\item \begin{enumerate}[(a)]\item We have that $\delta(L,M_1)=\delta(L,M_2)=2$ and $\delta(M_1,M_2)=4$. Lemma \ref{intersections1} with $d_1=2$ and  $d_2=2r-1$ shows that $$\Gamma_{\leq 2r-3 }(L)=\Gamma_{\leq 2r-1}(M_1)\cap \Gamma_{\leq 2r-1}(M_2).$$
Restricting these sets to their intersection with $\mathcal{P}$ yields the desired result.
\item This follows from noting that $\delta(v_1,v_2)$ is even and restricting the equality found in part 1 to the point set $\mathcal{P}$.
\end{enumerate}
\end{enumerate}
head: environment

label: starLemma
title: Lemma
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
\(\)
	\begin{enumerate}[(i)]
		\item We prove this by induction on \(d\). The base case \(d=1\) follows by taking $M=L$.
		Assume that the statement holds for some \(k\in \mathbb{N}\) with \(1\le k < m-1\) and consider the case \(d=k+1\). 
		Let \(L\in\mathcal{L}\) be an arbitrary line of \(\Gamma\). Then there exists an \(M\in \mathcal{L}_{\le 2k-2}(L)\) such that \(C\cap \mathcal{P}_{\le2k-1}(M) = C\cap \mathcal{P}_{1}(L)\). 
		
		We label the \(s+1\) points on \(M\) as \(\{v_1,v_2,\dots,v_{s+1}\}\). For each of these points \(v_i\) we can consider a line \(N_i\) through \(v_i\) and different from \(M\). Note that the lines $N_1,\ldots,N_{s+1}$ are mutually disjoint.
		
		By Corollary \ref{intersections2}(2a), we now observe that for any two of these lines \(N_i\) and \(N_j\) with \(i\neq j\), we have \[\mathcal{P}_{\le 2(k+1)-1}(N_i)\cap \mathcal{P}_{\le 2(k+1)-1}(N_j)= \mathcal{P}_{\le 2(k+1)-3}(M).\]
		
		Since  \(|C|<s+1\), at least one of the $s+1$ disjoint sets \(\mathcal{P}_{\le 2(k+1)-1}(N_i)\setminus \mathcal{P}_{\le 2(k+1)-3}(M) \), $i \in \{1,2,\ldots,s+1\}$, must have an empty intersection with \(C\). Without loss of generality, we may assume 
		\[(\mathcal{P}_{\le 2(k+1)-1}(N_1)\setminus \mathcal{P}_{\le 2(k+1)-3}(M)) \cap C = \emptyset.\]
		This means that 
		\[C\cap \mathcal{P}_{\le2(k+1)-1}(N_1) = C\cap \mathcal{P}_{\le2(k+1)-3}(M) = C\cap \mathcal{P}_{1}(L),\]
		 where we have invoked the induction hypothesis.
         
		Since \(M\in \mathcal{L}_{2k-2}(L)\) and \(N_1\in\mathcal{L}_{2}(M)\),  we see that \(N_1\in   \mathcal{L}_{2k-2+2}(L)=\mathcal{L}_{2k}(L)=\mathcal{L}_{2(k+1)-2}(L)\). The statement follows.
		
		\item Let \(L\in\mathcal{L}\) be an arbitrary line of \(\Gamma\). 
		From part (i), we know that there exists a line \(M\in \mathcal{L}_{\le 2d-2}(L)\) such that \(C\cap \mathcal{P}_{\le2d-1}(M) = C\cap \mathcal{P}_{1}(L)\).
		
		We label the \(s+1\) points on \(M\) as \(\{v_1,v_2,\dots,v_{s+1}\}\). 

		By Corollary \ref{intersections2}(2b), we have that for \(i\neq j\),  \[\mathcal{P}_{\le 2d}(v_i)\cap \mathcal{P}_{\le 2d}(v_j)= \mathcal{P}_{\le 2d-1}(M).\]
		
		Since \(|C|<s+1\) points, at least one of the disjoint  sets \(\mathcal{P}_{\le 2d}(v_i)\setminus \mathcal{P}_{\le 2d-1}(M) \) must have an empty intersection with \(C\). Without loss of generality, we may assume 
		\[(\mathcal{P}_{\le 2d}(v_1)\setminus \mathcal{P}_{\le 2d-1}(M)) \cap C = \emptyset.\]
		This means that 
		\[C\cap \mathcal{P}_{\le2d}(v_1) = C\cap \mathcal{P}_{\le2d-1}(M) = C\cap \mathcal{P}_{1}(L)\]
		
		Since $v_1\in \mathcal{P}_1(M)$ and $M\subseteq \mathcal{L}_{\leq 2d-2}(L)$, we see that \(v_1\in \mathcal{P}_{1}(M) \subseteq \mathcal{P}_{\leq 2d-1}(L)\) and the statement follows.\qedhere
	\end{enumerate}
head: environment

label: G4s
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{G4s}
	Let \(v\) be a point of \(\Gamma\). Then, every line \(L\) intersects \(\mathcal{P}_{\le 2m-2}(v)\) in either \(1\) or \(s+1\) points.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
By Corollary \ref{uniqueClosest}, \(L\) contains a unique point \(w\) closest to \(v\) and we know that \(\delta(v,w) \in \{0,2,\dots, 2m-2\}\).
	If \(\delta(v,w) < 2m-2\) then clearly all points on \(L\) are in \(\mathcal{P}_{\leq 2m-2}(v)\). If \(\delta(v,w) = 2m-2\) then all points on \(L\) different from $w$ are at distance \(2m\) from \(v\) and therefore not in \(\mathcal{P}_{\leq 2m-2}(v)\).
head: environment

label: smallC1
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{smallC1} Let \(B\) be a set of points of \(\Gamma\) such that
	\[\forall L\in \mathcal{L}: |\mathcal{P}_{1}(L)\cap B|\ge 1,\]
	then \(|B|\ge \frac{s^m t^m-1}{st-1}\).
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
We double count the following set:
	\[X := \{(v,L)\mid v\in B, L\in \mathcal{L}, v\mathtt{I} L\}.\]
	Each point in $B$ lies on \(t+1\) lines so we find \(|X|=|B|(t+1)\).
	Because there are \(|\mathcal{L}| = (1+t)\frac{s^m t^m-1}{st-1}\) lines (see for instance \cite{Hendrik}), each of which needs to contain at least one point of  \(B\) we find \(|X|\ge(1+t)\frac{s^m t^m-1}{st-1} \).
	Combining these results gives us \(|B|\ge \frac{s^m t^m-1}{st-1} \).
head: environment

label: smallC
title: Lemma
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Assume to the contrary that \(|C|<s+1\). 
	Lemma \ref{starLemma} (ii) with \(d=m-1\) tells us that 
	\[\forall L \in \mathcal{L}: \exists x \in \mathcal{P}_{\le 2m-3}(L):   C\cap \mathcal{P}_{\le2m-2}(x)=C\cap \mathcal{P}_{1}(L) .\]
	Since $\forall x$, $C\cap \mathcal{P}_{\le 2m-2}(x)\neq\emptyset$ , we deduce that
	\[\forall L \in \mathcal{L}: C\cap \mathcal{P}_{1}(L)\neq \emptyset.\]
	Using Lemma \ref{smallC1}, we find that $|C|\geq \frac{s^mt^m-1}{st-1}\geq s+1$, a contradiction.
head: environment

label: exists0
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{exists0} Assume that $s\leq t$. Let \(C\) be a set of points of size \(s+1\) and let \(x\) be an element of \(\Gamma\). Let \(d\in\{1,\dots,2m-2\}\).
	If \(\mathcal{P}_{\le d-1}(x)\cap C = \emptyset\) and 
	\[\exists y \in \Gamma_1(x): |\mathcal{P}_{\le d}(y)\cap C| \ge 2\] then
	\[\exists z \in \Gamma_1(x): \mathcal{P}_{\le d}(z)\cap C = \emptyset. \]
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Let \(z_1\) and \(z_2\) be two different elements in \( \Gamma_1(x)\).
	By Corollary  \ref{gammaProperties} and \ref{intersections2}(1),
	\[\mathcal{P}_{\le d}(z_1) \cap \mathcal{P}_{\le d}(z_2)\cap C = \mathcal{P}_{\le d-1}(x) \cap C= \emptyset.\] 
	Assume to the contrary that 
	\[\forall z \in \Gamma_1(x): |\mathcal{P}_{\le d}(z)\cap C| > 0, \]
then we find that \(|C|\ge |\Gamma_1(x)\setminus\{y\}| + 2 \).

There are either $s$ (when $x$ is a line) or $t$ (when $x$ is a point) elements in $\Gamma_1(x),$ different from $y$. 
    Hence, since  \(s\le t\) there are at least \(s\) elements in \(\Gamma_1(x)\) different from \(y\). 
	We find \(|C|\ge |\Gamma_1(x)\setminus\{y\}| + 2 \ge s+2\), a contradiction since $|C|=s+1$.
head: environment

label: traceLines
title: Lemma
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Assume to the contrary that there is an element \(y\) in \(\Gamma_{1}(x)\) with 
	\[\mathcal{P}_{d-1}(y)\cap C = \emptyset.\]
	We prove the following claim by induction on \(d'\):
	\[\forall d' \in \{d-1,\dots,2m-2\}:\exists z \in \Gamma_{\le d'-d +1}(y): \mathcal{P}_{\le d'}(z)\cap C = \emptyset.\]
	The base case \(d' = d-1\) follows by considering the point \(y\): since \(\Gamma_{\le d-2}(y)\) is a subset of \(\mathcal{P}_{\le d-1}(x)\), the statement follows from \(\mathcal{P}_{\le d-1}(x)\cap C = \emptyset\) and \(\mathcal{P}_{d-1}(y)\cap C = \emptyset\).
	
	Now assume that the statement holds for \(d' = k\) with \(d-1\le k<2m-2\). 
	We find an element \(z_k\) in \(\Gamma_{\le k-d+1}(y)\) such that \[\mathcal{P}_{\le k}(z_k)\cap C = \emptyset.\] 
	
	Since \(z_k\in \Gamma_{\le k-d+1}(y)\) we also get \(y \in \Gamma_{\le k-d+1}(z_k)\).
	Hence, there is an element \(y'\) in \(\Gamma_{1}(z_k)\) such that \(y \in \Gamma_{\le k-d}(y')\). This implies that \[\mathcal{P}_d(x) \subseteq \mathcal{P}_{\le d+1}(y) \subseteq \mathcal{P}_{\le k+1}(y').\]
	Therefore, \(\mathcal{P}_{\le k+1}(y')\) contains at least two points of \(C\).
	We are now ready to use Lemma \ref{exists0} with \(x=z_k\) and \(y=y'\). This implies the existence of an element \(z_{k+1}\) in \(\Gamma_1(z_k)\subseteq \Gamma_{\le k-d+2}(y)\) such that \[\mathcal{P}_{\le k+1}(z_{k+1})\cap C = \emptyset.\]
	This proves our claim.
	By setting \(d'=2m-2\), we now find a contradiction with the assumption that $C$ is an $\mathcal{X}-$blocking set.
head: environment

label: pointsAtDist
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{pointsAtDist} Assume that \(s\le t\). 
	Let \(C\) be a set of points of size \(s+1\). 
	Let \(x\) be an element of \(\Gamma\) such that for some \(d\in\{1,\dots,2m-2\}\) the following hold:
	\begin{itemize}
		\item \(\mathcal{P}_{\le d-2}(x)\) contains no points of \(C\).
		\item $C$ is a $\mathcal{Y}$- blocking set where $\mathcal{Y}=\{\mathcal{P}_{d-1}(y)\mid y\in \Gamma_1(x)\}.$
        
                                                                                                                              
	\end{itemize}
	Then, \(C\subseteq \mathcal{P}_d(x)\) and if \(x\) is a point, then \(s=t\).
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Corollary \ref{intersections2}(1) shows that for any two elements \(y_1\) and \(y_2\) in \(\Gamma_{1}(x)\) \[ \Gamma_{\le d-1}(y_1)\cap\Gamma_{\le d-1}(y_2)=\Gamma_{\le d - 2}(x).\]
This implies that 
\[\mathcal{P}_{d-1}(y_1)\cap\mathcal{P}_{d-1}(y_2) \subseteq \mathcal{P}_{\leq d-2}(x).\]
Since $\mathcal{P}_{\leq d-2}\cap C=\emptyset$ we see that for every $y\in \Gamma_1(x),$ the set \(\mathcal{P}_{d-1}(y)\setminus\mathcal{P}_{d-2}(x)\) contains a different point of \(C\), and the points obtained in this way are mutually distinct. We find that $s+1=|C|\geq |\Gamma_1(x)|$. If $x$ is a point, $|\Gamma_1(x)|=t+1$, and by our assumption, $t\geq s$, so it follows that in this case $s=t$.
Furthermore, it follows that in both the case where $x$ a point or $x$ is a line, each of the sets  \(\mathcal{P}_{d-1}(y)\setminus\mathcal{P}_{d-2}(x)\) contains exactly one point of \(C\), and $C$ does not contain any further points. It follows that $C\subseteq \mathcal{P}_{\leq d}(x)$, and since $\mathcal{P}_{\leq d-2}(x)\cap C=\emptyset$, $C\subseteq \mathcal{P}_d(x)$.
head: environment

title: Definition
body_md:
A {\em distance $d$-trace} \(T_{d,x,y}\), where \(d\in \{1,\dots,m\}\), is a non-empty set of points such that there exist opposite elements \(x\) and \(y\) in \(\mathcal{P}\cup\mathcal{L}\) with 
	\[T_{d,x,y} = \mathcal{P}_{d}(x)\cap\mathcal{P}_{2m-d}(y).\]
head: environment

title: Remark
body_md: Note that $x$ and $y$ play a different role in the definition so unless $d=m$, the distance $d$-trace determined by $x$ and $y$ is different from the distance $d$-trace determined by $y$ and $x$.
head: environment

title: Remark
body_md: The point set of a line is an example of a distance trace: take $d=1$, $x=L$ and $M$ any line opposite to $L$, then $T_{1,L,M}=\mathcal{P}_1(L)\cap \mathcal{P}_{2m-1}(M)=\mathcal{P}_1(L).$
head: environment

label: distanceTraces
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{distanceTraces}Assume that \(s\le t\).
Let $C$ be an $\mathcal{X}$-blocking set. Then $|C|\geq s+1$. If equality holds then $C$ is a distance $d$-trace $T_{d,x,y}$ for some opposite elements $x,y$ of $\Gamma$ and some $d\in \{1,\ldots,m\}$. 
                                                                                                                                                                                      
 Furthermore, if equality holds and $s<t$, then $d$ is odd.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Let \(z_1\neq z_2\) be two points of \(C\) such that $\delta(z_1,z_2)\leq 
    \delta(u,v)$ for all $u\neq v$ points of $C$.
                                          
    
    By the axioms of the generalised \(2m\)-gon $\Gamma$, there exists an ordinary \(2m\)-gon $\Gamma'$ containing \(z_1\) and \(z_2\). Since \(z_1\) and \(z_2\) are both points, the distance between them is even, and we can find opposite elements \(x\) and \(y\) in $\Gamma'$ such that:
	\begin{itemize}
		\item \(z_1,z_2 \in \mathcal{P}_d(x)\)
		\item \(z_1,z_2 \in \mathcal{P}_{2m-d}(y)\)
	\end{itemize}
	for \(d=\frac{\delta(z_1,z_2)}{2}\).
	
If \(\mathcal{P}_{\le d-1}(x)\) would contain a point of \(C\), then \(z_1\) and \(z_2\) would not have been at the minimal distance. We can therefore use Lemma \ref{traceLines} and Lemma \ref{pointsAtDist} to conclude that all points of \(C\) are contained in \(\mathcal{P}_{d}(x)\).
Since \(x\) and \(y\) are opposite, \(\mathcal{P}_{\le d}(x)\cap \mathcal{P}_{\le 2m-d-1}(y) = \emptyset\) and we get that \(\mathcal{P}_{\le 2m-d-1}(y)\) can not contain any point of \(C\). Again, from lemma \ref{traceLines} and lemma \ref{pointsAtDist}, we can conclude that \(C\subseteq \mathcal{P}_{2m-d}(y)\). 
We now have \(C\subseteq \mathcal{P}_{d}(x)\cap\mathcal{P}_{2m-d}(y)\) proving the statement.
head: environment

label: rem:traces
title: Remark
body_md:
\label{rem:traces} As seen before, when $d=1$, we consider opposite lines $x,y$, and $T_{1,x,y}$ is the set of points on the line $x$. 
In the case of weak generalised quadrangles, the distance $2$-trace is the set of points collinear to two non-collinear points. When the generalised quadrangle is $W(3,q)$, the distance $2$-trace is given by the points of a line of the ambient projective space (see also Remark \ref{remark:W3q}), and in the case of $\mathcal{Q}(4,q)$, this set is the point set of a conic in the ambient space. For the generalised hexagon $\mathsf{H}(q)$ a similar situation arises. It is well-known that there is an embedding of \(\mathsf{H}(q)\) in $\mathcal{Q}(6,q)$, which is a polar space embedded in $\mathrm{PG}(6,q)$.
This embedding has the property that for two points $v,w$ in $\mathsf{H}(q)$, $\delta(v,w)=4$ if and only if $v$ and $w$ are collinear in $\mathcal{Q}(6,q)$ but not in $\mathsf{H}(q)$.
This allows us to describe the distance $d$-traces in $\mathsf{H}(q)$ geometrically: when $d=2$, we consider opposite points $x,y$. We find that $T_{2,x,y}$ is the set of $q+1$ points on a line of $\mathcal{Q}(6,q)$ that is not a line of $\mathsf{H}(q)$. The set of points $\mathcal{P}_{\leq 4}(v)$ is contained in the hyperplane $v^\perp$, where $\perp$ denotes the polarity corresponding to $\mathcal{Q}(6,q)$. The line $T_{2,x,y}$ and the hyperplane $v^\perp$ in $\mathrm{PG}(6,q)$ always intersect in at least a point, which is contained in $\mathcal{Q}(6,q)$, and hence, in $\mathsf{H}(q)$. We deduce that in this case, $T_{2,x,y}$ forms an $\mathcal{X}$-blocking set.
When $d=3$, we consider again opposite lines $x,y$. The set of points at distance $3$ from both $x$ and $y$ is the set of $q+1$ points of $x^\perp\cap y^\perp$, where $\perp$ denotes the polarity corresponding to $\mathcal{Q}(6,q)$. These $q+1$ points form a conic in $\mathrm{PG}(6,q)$.
head: environment

title: Remark
body_md:
The complement of the set $\mathcal{P}_{\leq 2m-2}(v)$ is precisely the set of points at distance $2m$ of $v$, the set of points opposite to $v$. It follows that an $\mathcal{X}$-blocking set is a set of points $B$ such that there is no point opposite all of the points of $B$. 
    This point of view can be used to derive similar results for other point-line incidence geometries and to introduce the related concept of a  {\em geometric} line (see \cite{Kasikova}): this is a set of points such that each point is not opposite all or one point of the set. Note though that the definition of an $\mathcal{X}$-blocking set does not have fixed intersection sizes.
head: environment

title: Definition
head: environment

title: Lemma
body_md: Let $x$ be a projective point of $\Gamma$, let $y$ be a point which is opposite to $x$ and let $T=T_{2,x,y}$ be the distance $2$-trace determined by $x$ and $y$. Then $T$ is an $\mathcal{X}$-blocking set.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Let $\Gamma'=(\mathcal{P}',\mathcal{L}',I')$ be the projective plane which is the perp-geometry determined by the projective point $x$. We need to show that for all $v\in \mathcal{P}$, $\mathcal{P}_{\leq 2m-2}(v)\cap T_{2,x,y}\neq \emptyset$. If $v$ is opposite $x$, then $T_{2,x,v}$ and $T_{2,x,y}$ are lines of $\Gamma'$, and since $\Gamma'$ is a projective plane, these two lines have a point $w$ of $\Gamma'$ in common. Since $w$ is a point of $T_{2,x,v}$, it follows that $w\in \mathcal{P}_{\leq 2m-2}(v)\cap T_{2,x,y}.$
    
    If $v$ and $x$ are not opposite, $\delta(v,x)\leq 2m-2$. The second point of a shortest path from $x$ to $v$, say $r$, is contained in one of the lines through $x$, say $L$. We have that $r$ is contained in $\mathcal{P}_{\leq 2m-4}(v)$, and since $L$ is a line of $\Gamma'$, it meets $T_{2,x,y}$, which is a line of $\Gamma'$ too, in a point $s$ of $\Gamma'$. Since $\delta(r,s)=2$, and $r\in \mathcal{P}_{\leq 2m-4}(v)$ it follows that $s\in \mathcal{P}_{\leq 2m-2}(v)\cap T_{2,x,y}.$ 
    We conclude that $T_{2,x,y}$ is an $\mathcal{X}-$ blocking set.
head: environment

label: remark:W3q
title: Remark
body_md:
\label{remark:W3q} For certain families of weak generalised polygons, the existence of projective points is very easy to deduce. Consider for example the generalised quadrangle $W(3,q)$ which is embedded in $\mathrm{PG}(3,q)$, let $x$ be a point of $W(3,q)$ and let $\perp$ denote the associated polarity. The perp-geometry of $x$ is simply the point-line geometry of the projective plane $\pi=x^\perp$: the sets $T_{2,x,y}$ are given by the lines obtained as intersection of the planes $x^\perp$ and $y^\perp$ in $\mathrm{PG}(3,q)$. Hence, every point of $W(3,q)$ is a projective point.
It is also not too hard to show that the points of \(\mathsf{H}(q)\) are projective, but many interesting questions related to the existence of projective points and characterisations of weak generalised polygons based on the existence of such points are wide open.

label: cxDef
title: Definition
body_md:
\label{cxDef}
	Let \(v\) be a point of \(\Gamma\). 
	
	We can define the following element of \(\mathbb{F}\mathcal{P}\) determined by \(v\):
	\[\mathfrak{c}_{v} := \sum_{k=0}^{m-1} \left(\sum_{j=0}^{m-k-1} (-s)^{j}\right)\mathfrak{i}_{\mathcal{P}_{2k}(v)}. \]
	The support of this vector is contained in \(\mathcal{P}_{\le 2m-2}(v)\).
head: environment

title: Remark
body_md:
We see that in a specific setting, such as a weak generalised hexagon, the expression from the previous definition becomes: 
\[\mathfrak{c}_{v} := (s^2-s+1)\mathfrak{i}_{\mathcal{P}_0(v)} + (-s+1)\mathfrak{i}_{\mathcal{P}_2(v)}+ \mathfrak{i}_{\mathcal{P}_4(v)}. \]
Recall that the value \(s^2-s+1\) or \(-s+1\) could evaluate to \(0\) over \(\mathbb{F}\) (see Remark \ref{possibleZero}), but if this does not happen, the support of $\mathfrak{c}_{v}$ is precisely $\mathcal{P}_{\le 2m-2}(v)$
head: environment

label: cx1
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{cx1} For all points $v$ and all lines $L$ in $\Gamma$ we have
	                                               
    \(\langle\mathfrak{c}_{v}, \mathfrak{i}_L\rangle = 1\).
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Let \(L\) be a line of \(\Gamma\). By Corollary \ref{uniqueClosest}, there exists a unique point \(w\) on \(L\) closest to \(v\). 
	Let \(d = \delta(v,w)\). Observe that $d$ is even, that \(d \le 2m-2\), and that 
	\begin{align*}
		\langle\mathfrak{c}_{v}, \mathfrak{i}_L\rangle 
		&= \sum_{\{z\in\mathcal{P}\mid z\mathtt{I} L\}} \mathfrak{c}_{v}(z)\\
	\end{align*}

	If \(d = 2m-2\) then we find
	\begin{align*}
		\langle\mathfrak{c}_{v}, \mathfrak{i}_L\rangle 
		&= \mathfrak{c}_{v}(w) \\
		&= \sum_{j=0}^{0} (-s)^{j} \\
		&= 1.
	\end{align*}
	
	If \(d<2m-2\) then
	\begin{align*}
		\langle\mathfrak{c}_{v}, \mathfrak{i}_L\rangle 
		&= \left(\sum_{j=0}^{m-1-\frac{d}{2}} (-s)^{j}\right) + s\left(\sum_{j=0}^{m-1-\frac{d}{2}-1} (-s)^{j}\right) \\
		&= \left(\sum_{j=1}^{m-1-\frac{d}{2}} (-s)^{j}\right) + 1 - \left(\sum_{j=0}^{m-2-\frac{d}{2}} (-s)^{j+1}\right) \\
		&= \left(\sum_{j=1}^{m-1-\frac{d}{2}} (-s)^{j}\right) + 1 - \left(\sum_{j'=1}^{m-1-\frac{d}{2}} (-s)^{j'}\right) \\
		&= 1.
	\end{align*}

label: AllEq
title: Corollary
body_md: \label{AllEq}Let \(\mathfrak{c}\in \mathfrak{C}_\mathbb{F}\) and let  \( v, w \) be points of \(\Gamma\). Then \( \langle \mathfrak{c}, \mathfrak{c}_{v} \rangle = \langle \mathfrak{c}, \mathfrak{c}_w \rangle\).

title: Proof
body_md: Lemma \ref{cxcy} shows that \( \langle \mathfrak{c}, \mathfrak{c}_{v} - \mathfrak{c}_w \rangle = 0\) for all \(\mathfrak{c}\in \mathfrak{C}_\mathbb{F}\).

label: existsEmpty
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{existsEmpty}
Let \(\mathfrak{c}\in \mathbb{F}\mathcal{P}\) and let \(C\) be the support of \(\mathfrak{c}\).
If \(|C|<s+1\) then
\[\exists v \in \mathcal{P}: \langle \mathfrak{c}, \mathfrak{c}_{v}\rangle = 0.\]
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
By Lemma \ref{smallC} we know that there exists a point \(v\) such that 
	\[|\mathcal{P}_{\le 2m-2}(v)\cap C| = 0.\]
	Since the support of \(\mathfrak{c}_{v}\) is contained in \(\mathcal{P}_{\le 2m-2}(v)\), the statement follows.
head: environment

title: Definition
body_md:
Let \(L\) be a line and \(\mathfrak{f}\) an element of \(\mathbb{F}\mathcal{P}\).
	We say that \(L\) is \textbf{covered} by \(\mathfrak{f}\) if for each point \(v\) on \(L\) we have \(\mathfrak{f}(v) \neq 0\). Equivalently, $L$ is covered by $\mathfrak{f}$ if and only if \(|\text{supp}(\mathfrak{i}_L\cdot\mathfrak{f})| = s+1\).
head: environment

label: smallcx
title: Lemma
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Let \(w\) be a point of \(C\) and assume that \(|C|\le t+1\).
	It follows that at least one of the \(t+1\) lines through \(w\), say $M$, does not contain a second point of \(C\). Our assumption implies that there exists a point \(v\in\mathcal{P}\) such that \(|\text{supp}(\mathfrak{c}_{v}\cdot \mathfrak{i}_M)| = s+1 \text{ and } \langle \mathfrak{c}, \mathfrak{c}_{v}\cdot\mathfrak{i}_M \rangle = 0 \). Since \(\langle \mathfrak{c}, \mathfrak{c}_{v}\cdot\mathfrak{i}_M \rangle = \langle \mathfrak{c}, \mathfrak{c}_{v}\cdot\mathfrak{i}_{\{w\}} \rangle = \mathfrak{c}(w)\cdot \mathfrak{c}_{v}(w)\) where both \(\mathfrak{c}(w)\) and \(\mathfrak{c}_{x}(w)\) are elements of \(\mathbb{F}\) different from \(0\), this is a contradiction.
head: environment

label: smallc
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{smallc}
	Let \(\mathfrak{c}\in \mathbb{F}\mathcal{P}\) and let \(C\) be the support of \(\mathfrak{c}\).
	If \(|C|<s+1\) then
	\[\forall L \in \mathcal{L}:\exists v \in \mathcal{P}_{\le2m-3}(L): \mathfrak{c}\cdot\mathfrak{c}_{v} = \mathfrak{c}\cdot\mathfrak{c}_{v}\cdot\mathfrak{i}_L.\]
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
By Lemma \(\ref{starLemma}\) (ii) with \(d=m-1\) we get:
	\[\forall L \in \mathcal{L}: \exists v \in \mathcal{P}_{\le 2m-3}(L): C\cap \mathcal{P}_{\le2m-2}(v) = C\cap \mathcal{P}_{1}(L).\]
	Therefore, \[\mathfrak{i}_{C\cap \mathcal{P}_{\le2m-2}(v)}= \mathfrak{i}_{C\cap \mathcal{P}_{1}(L)}.\]
	Which implies that
	\[\mathfrak{c}\cdot\mathfrak{c}_{v} = \mathfrak{c}\cdot\mathfrak{i}_C\cdot\mathfrak{c}_{v}\cdot\mathfrak{i}_{\mathcal{P}_{\le2m-2}(v)} = \mathfrak{c}\cdot\mathfrak{c}_v\cdot\mathfrak{i}_{C\cap \mathcal{P}_{\le2m-2}(v)}= \mathfrak{c}\cdot\mathfrak{c}_{v}\cdot \mathfrak{i}_{C\cap \mathcal{P}_{1}(L)} = \mathfrak{c}\cdot\mathfrak{c}_{v}\cdot\mathfrak{i}_C\cdot \mathfrak{i}_L = \mathfrak{c}\cdot\mathfrak{c}_{v}\cdot\mathfrak{i}_L.\]
head: environment

label: alsoLines
title: Lemma
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
The set $C\setminus\{v\}$ has size $s$, so we can invoke Lemma \ref{starLemma} with $d=m-1$ to deduce that there exists a \(w\in\mathcal{P}_{\le 2m-3}(L)\) such that \[(C\setminus \{v\}) \cap \mathcal{P}_{\le 2m-2}(w) = (C\setminus \{v\}) \cap \mathcal{P}_{1}(L).\]
	Because \(v\in C\cap\mathcal{P}_{\le 2m-2}(w)\cap\mathcal{P}_{1}(L)\), we get
	\[C \cap \mathcal{P}_{\le 2m-2}(w) = C \cap \mathcal{P}_{1}(L).\]
	The statement now follows since
	\[\mathfrak{c}_w\cdot\mathfrak{c} = \mathfrak{c}_w\cdot\mathfrak{c}\cdot\mathfrak{i}_{\mathcal{P}_{\le 2m-2}(w)}\cdot\mathfrak{i}_C = \mathfrak{c}_w\cdot\mathfrak{c}\cdot\mathfrak{i}_{\mathcal{P}_{1}(L)}\cdot\mathfrak{i}_C = \mathfrak{c}_w\cdot \mathfrak{c}\cdot \mathfrak{i}_L.\]
head: environment

label: neverEmpty
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{neverEmpty} Let $s\leq t$.
	Let \(\mathfrak{c}\in \mathfrak{C}_\mathbb{F}\) and let \(C\) be the support of \(\mathfrak{c}\). Assume that \(|C|=s+1\) and that  
	\[\forall v\in \mathcal{P}: \text{supp}(\mathfrak{c}_v) = \mathcal{P}_{\leq 2m-2}(v)\]
	Then,
	\[\forall v\in \mathcal{P}: \langle \mathfrak{c}_v ,\mathfrak{c}\rangle \neq 0.\]
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Assume that there exists a point \(v\in \mathcal{P}\) such that \(\langle \mathfrak{c}_{v} ,\mathfrak{c}\rangle = 0\). By Corollary \ref{AllEq}, we then have \[\forall w\in \mathcal{P}: \langle \mathfrak{c}_w ,\mathfrak{c}\rangle = 0.\] Now let \(v\) be a point of \(C\). Since we assume \(s\le t\), and \(|C\setminus\{v\}| = s\), at least one of the lines through \(v\) does not contain a second point \(C\). Let \(L\) be such a line. By Lemma \ref{alsoLines}, we find that 
	\[\exists w \in \mathcal{P}_{\le 2m-3}(L): \langle \mathfrak{c}_w\cdot \mathfrak{i}_L ,\mathfrak{c}\rangle = \langle \mathfrak{c}_w,\mathfrak{c}\rangle = 0.\] 
    
	This means that 
	\[\mathfrak{c}_w(v)\cdot\mathfrak{c}(v) = 0.\]
	Because \(\mathbb{F}\) is a field and both \(\mathfrak{c}_w(v)\) and \(\mathfrak{c}(v)\) are assumed to be non-zero, this forms a contradiction.
head: environment

label: main
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{main}
	Let \(\Gamma\) be a finite thick generalised \(2m\)-gon of order \((s,t)\) with \(s\le t\) and \(m>1\). 
	Let \(\mathbb{F}\) be a field such that none of the $m-1$ elements in 
    \[\left\{\sum_{j=0}^{k} (-s)^{j} \mid  1\le k \leq m-1, k\in \mathbb{Z}\right\}\]
    are \(0\) over \(\mathbb{F}\). 
	Then the minimum weight of \(\mathfrak{C}_\mathbb{F}(\Gamma)\) is \(s+1\) and the support of any minimum weight code word is a distance $d$-trace $T_{d,x,y}$ for some $d\in \{1,\ldots,m-1\}$.

    Furthermore, if $s<t$, then $d$ is odd. In particular, if $\Gamma$ is a thick generalised quadrangle of order $(s,t)$ with $s<t$, then every minimum weight code word of $\mathfrak{C}_\mathbb{F}$ is a scalar multiple of the incidence vector of a line.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Let \(\mathfrak{c}\in\mathfrak{C}_\mathbb{F}\)  be a codeword with support $C$ and assume to the contrary that $|C|<s
    +1$. 
	
	By Lemma \ref{existsEmpty}, 
	\[\exists v \in \mathcal{P}: \langle \mathfrak{c}, \mathfrak{c}_{v} \rangle = 0,\]
	while Corollary \ref{AllEq} implies that 
	\[\forall v, w \in \mathcal{P}: \langle \mathfrak{c}, \mathfrak{c}_{v} \rangle = \langle \mathfrak{c}, \mathfrak{c}_w\rangle. \]
	We conclude that
	\[\forall v\in \mathcal{P}: \langle \mathfrak{c}, \mathfrak{c}_{v}\rangle = 0.\]
	From Lemma \ref{smallc} we get
	\[\forall L \in \mathcal{L}:\exists v \in \mathcal{P}_{\le2m-3}(L): \mathfrak{c}\cdot\mathfrak{c}_{v} = \mathfrak{c}\cdot\mathfrak{c}_{v}\cdot\mathfrak{i}_L.\]
	Combining this, we find 
	\[\forall L \in \mathcal{L}:\exists v \in \Gamma_{\le2m-3}(L): \langle \mathfrak{c},\mathfrak{c}_{v}\rangle = \langle \mathfrak{c}\cdot \mathfrak{c}_{v}, \mathbf{1} \rangle = \langle \mathfrak{c}\cdot \mathfrak{c}_{v}\cdot \mathfrak{i}_L, \mathbf{1} \rangle = \langle \mathfrak{c},\mathfrak{c}_{v}\cdot \mathfrak{i}_L\rangle = 0.\]
	The condition on \(\mathbb{F}\) implies that for all $v\in \mathcal{P}$, $supp(\mathfrak{c}_{v})=\mathcal{P}_{\leq 2m-2}(v)$. Since all points on a line that lies at distance at most $2m-3$ from a point $v$ lie at distance at most $2m-2$ of $v$, we see that all lines at distance at most \(2m-3\) from \(v\) are covered by \(\mathfrak{c}_{v}\) i.e.:
	\[\forall L\in \mathcal{L}: \forall v \in \mathcal{P}_{\le 2m-3}(L): |\text{supp}(\mathfrak{i}_L\cdot\mathfrak{c}_{v})| = s+1.\]
	Therefore, the conditions for Lemma \ref{smallcx} are fulfilled, which gives us \(|C|>t+1\). This contradicts the assumptions that $|C|<s+1$ and \(s\le t\).
	
	Since for any line \(L\in \mathcal{L}\), the codeword \(\mathfrak{i}_L\) has weight \(s+1\), we have shown that the minimum weight of $\mathfrak{C}_\mathbb{F}$ is $s+1$.

    Now assume that $|C|=s+1$. The condition on $\mathbb{F}$ shows that we can invoke Lemma \ref{neverEmpty} to find that $C$ forms an $\mathcal{X}$-blocking set.  Theorem \ref{distanceTraces} now shows that $C$ is a distance trace $T_{d,x,y}$. Furthermore, if $s<t$, then $d$ is odd. If additionally $\Gamma$ is a weak generalised quadrangle, then $m=2$, so since $d\in \{1,\ldots,m\}$ is odd, only the possibility $T_{1,x,y}$ occurs: the support $C$ is the point set of a line. 
    Now assume that $C$ is the point set of a line $L$. Let $v$ be a point of $L$. Consider the vector $\mathfrak{c}-\mathfrak{c}(v)\mathfrak{i}_L$. This is a linear combination of code words in $\mathfrak{C}_\mathbb{F}$, so it is a code word of $\mathfrak{C}_\mathbb{F}$, but its weight is at most $s$. Therefore, it is the zero vector. It follows that $\mathfrak{c}=\mathfrak{c}(v)\mathfrak{i}_L$.

title: Remark
body_md: We could state Theorem \ref{main} for finite weak generalised \(2m\)-gons, but the requirement \(1-s\neq 0\), together with \(s\le t\) forces the \(2m\)-gon to be thick since this implies that every point and every line is incident with at least three other elements (see Remark \ref{thickAlt}).
head: environment

title: Remark
body_md:
The condition on the field $\mathbb{F}$ in Theorem ef{main} boils down to the following: for finite thick generalised quadrangles, the condition \(s
eq 1\) in $\mathbb{F}$, is automatically fulfilled by being thick, for finite thick generalised hexagons, we have the additional requirement \(s^2-s+1
eq 0\) in $\mathbb{F}$, and for finite thick generalised octagons we require \(0
otin \{-s^3+s^2-s+1, s^2-s+1\}\) in $\mathbb{F}$. 
    In particular, the classical case, where we study the $p$-ary code of a polygon embedded in $\mathrm{PG}(n,q)$, $q=p^h$, $p$ prime, is included in the theorem since in that case, $s=q=0$ in \(\mathbb{F}=\mathbb{F}_p\).
head: environment

title: Remark
body_md: After presenting this work, we became aware of current ongoing research  that is expected to contain a slightly stronger version of Theorem \ref{distanceTraces} for the case of generalised hexagons \cite{SiraHendrik}. In this paper, which is currently still in preparation, the condition $s\leq t$ would not be present.
